thread.title: AT&T Merger Makes Telecoms Attractive

author: Lawrence Carrel
title: AT&T Merger Makes Telecoms Attractive

organizations.name: at&t merger makes telecoms attractive at&t
richard j. leon of u.s. district court

text:
AT&T's (T) $85.4 billion blockbuster merger with Time Warner (TWX) went through because a federal judge overruled an out-of-character antitrust move by the Trump Administration's Department of Justice. "The judge, Richard J. Leon of U.S. District Court in Washington, said the Justice Department had not proved that the telecom company’s acquisition of Time Warner would lead to fewer choices for consumers and higher prices for television and internet services," according to the New York Times.
The combined company will be a media and telecommunications powerhouse. It will own CNN and a wireless and satellite network to stream on mobile devices.
Harley Lance Kaplan, managing principle, for Beta Industries, a financial planning firm in Sherborn, Mass., has been spending a lot of time studying the telecom sector for value plays. He said this ruling, which suddenly allows vertical acquisitions may allow content companies to go in and buy telecommunications assets, when previously they had been worried about the administration's antimerger stance.
Kaplan, whose claim to fame was telling people to buy Google (GOOG) and Apple (AAPL) in Barron's in early 2009, said AT&T is a long-term buy after falling 6% on the deal going through. The stock is down 15% from the start of the year.
Kaplan said the Dallas-based AT&T needed to do something: "It said, 'content is expensive, so let's just buy something'." He thinks the merger should quickly be accretive to the bottom line. In 2017, Time Warner posted a profit of $5.2 billion on revenue of $31.7 billion. He added AT&T will protect its $2 annual dividend, which after the stock drop is now yielding 6.2%.
Most analysts think the next big media deal is between Comcast (CMCSA) and Disney (DIS), which are both battling for ownership of 21st Century Fox (FOXA).
Kaplan instead is looking at the old, unloved landline telecoms and sees huge value plays. He said the copper and fiber wires that move data are the information highways of the future and that they are valuable assets that are seriously being undervalued. He views these companies two ways. The old way is for talking, voice communications over landline phones. This business is dying as more and more people cut the cord for cell phones and voice over Internet. However, Kaplan says we're in the early states of home automation, artificial intelligence, and transportation automation.
"Why do you think Amazon.com (AMZN) bought Whole Foods?" asked Kaplan "Because you'll have monitors in your homes and your refrigerators will buy your food when you run low. These companies are going to run the security systems for our homes. And don't even mention holograms. The amount of bandwidth that is going to be necessary in the future is much more than we have now. You're still going to need copper and fiber. Wireless won't be able to handle it all. So, I think telecoms are a tremendous value based on future expectations."
He likes Centurylink (CTL), which merged with Level 3 Communications at the end of 2017. CenturyLink, based in Monroe, LA, was mostly legacy landlines and DSL, gained in Level 3, one of the world's largest Internet networks. He said the company understands the backbone of networks and is growing in the right sectors.
He bought CenturyLink for the total return, dividend and capital appreciation. With an annual dividend of $2.16, at $18.13 a share, that's a whopping yield of 12%. Yields that high usually mean something's wrong with the company or it's going to soon get cut.
But Kaplan said the stock took a hit because of the merger, but it will be accretive to earnings in the next six months. First-quarter revenues decreased 1.5% to $5.9 billion, but first-quarter cash flow nearly doubled to $941 million. Management expects free cash flow for the year between $3.15 billion and $3.35 billion, more than enough to cover the $2.3 billion needed for the dividend. Adjusted earnings before interest taxes depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) should be between $8.75 and $8.95 billion
"I'm not expecting this company to be around for the next five years. I think there are other people who know how to take this to the next level," said Kaplan. "My valuation is a market cap of $35 billion to $40 billion. It should be double where it is today. " On Monday, the company's market capitalization was $19.6 billion.
An even more speculative play is Frontier Communications (FTR). Based in Norwalk, CT., Frontier is mostly landlines and truly is dying. It has actually given up its dividend. But Kaplan said this is a takeover play purely for the assets. Frontier's big problem is $19 billion in long-term debt, but only $617 million in market cap. At $7 it's not expensive, but it's highly risky.
A dividend play outside the telecom industry is Global Partners (GLP). This master limited partnership (MLP) from Waltham, Mass., transports oil and gas. It's buying gas stations and convenience stores across New England. It currently pays an annual dividend of $1.85, which at $17.10 a share, is a 10.8% yield. Kaplan said this is a great value too.
